correctness.rationale: Write \(A=K[y,z][x;\delta]\) with \(\delta(y)=z\) and \(\delta(z)=\gamma y\). Bell--Li's \(p\)-polynomial gives \(c=x^4+\gamma x^2\) central in characteristic \(2\). Reducing uniquely to \(\sum_{i<4} r_i x^i\) over \(R[c]\), the formulas \([x^2,a]=\delta^2(a)\) and \([x^3,a]=\delta(a)x^2+\delta^2(a)x+\delta^3(a)\) show that commuting with \(y\) forces \(r_3=0\). Commuting with \(y\) and \(z\) then gives a \(2\times2\) system for \(r_1,r_2\) with nonzero determinant \(\gamma(z^2+\gamma y^2)\), so \(r_1=r_2=0\). As \(R\) is free over \(K[y^2,z^2]\) on \(1,y,z,yz\) and \(\delta\) kills only the scalar-basis coefficient, \(\ker\delta=K[y^2,z^2]\). Thus \(Z(A)=K[y^2,z^2,c]\). PBW leading terms yield algebraic independence and a 16-element central basis; central localization is a 16-dimensional division algebra, so PI degree is \(4\).
